featuredDrafts.title: The modifying effect of work-care role conflict on the effectiveness of carer support: Results from the Australian Draw Care randomised clinical trial
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: People who care for a family member with dementia alongside paid work often experience role conflict. This study explores whether work-care role conflict (WCRC) modifies the effectiveness of Draw Care, an online and culturally-adapted carer support intervention.  Secondary exploratory analysis of a single-blind, parallel-group trial (August 2023–November 2024) that compared Draw Care against waitlist control in adult carers from diverse linguistic backgrounds. To formally test whether WCRC moderated the effect of the Draw-Care intervention, we ran a full-sample linear mixed model that included a three-way interaction between time-point, treatment group and an indicator of WCRC. WCRC was operationalised as self-report of missed work or reduced productivity due to competing care and employment demands. Outcomes included carer burden, mood, quality of life, and productivity/ activity impairment at 6 and 12 weeks.  Forty-two of 93 carers reported WCRC. Reductions in caregiver burden due to treatment at 6 weeks (-10.00; 95% CI -19.70 to -0.31, p = 0.043) and 12 weeks (-9.56; 95% CI -18.83 to -0.29, p = 0.043) were significantly larger in participants with WCRC than without. This moderating effect of WCRC was driven by a robust, absolute reduction in caregiver burden in intervention group participants with WCRC over the initial 6 weeks (-7.19, 95%CI: -12.72 to -1.67, p = 0.011), with much of this improvement preserved at 12 weeks (-6.85, 95%CI: -12.17 to -1.53, p = 0.012).  WCRC appears to modify the effectiveness of Draw Care, suggesting that the intervention may be particularly helpful for carers navigating role conflict.

featuredDrafts.title: Associations of exercise snack–related step metrics with peripheral artery disease in older women: a cross-sectional study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Peripheral artery disease is a common vascular condition associated with impaired physical function and reduced quality of life in older adults. Although step volume and stepping intensity have been linked to cardiovascular health, the associations of intensity-specific step counts, cadence, and short-bout step accumulation with peripheral artery disease remain unclear. The concept of “exercise snacks,” characterized by brief, intermittent bouts of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, provides a useful framework for examining such activity patterns in free-living settings. This study examined the associations of objectively measured step counts, cadence, and bout-specific step accumulation with peripheral artery disease among community-dwelling older women.  This cross-sectional study included 1053 community-dwelling women aged 60–70 years from the Physical Activity and Health in Older Women Study. Step-based metrics were assessed using a waist-worn ActiGraph accelerometer over seven consecutive days. Steps were categorized as light-intensity physical activity or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. Step cadence and bout-specific step accumulation (≥ 3, ≥ 5, and ≥ 10 min) were also derived. Peripheral artery disease was defined as an ankle–brachial index ≤ 0.90. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to evaluate associations between step-based metrics and peripheral artery disease. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using the lower ankle–brachial index value from either leg as a continuous outcome and supplementary parsimonious regression models to reduce the potential influence of model overfitting.  After full adjustment, more steps accumulated during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (odds ratio = 0.696, 95% confidence interval: 0.531–0.912, P = 0.009) and higher cadence during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (odds ratio = 0.967, 95% confidence interval: 0.952–0.983, P  Higher moderate-to-vigorous physical activity–related step counts, faster cadence, and greater accumulation of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity in short bouts were associated with lower odds of peripheral artery disease among older women, whereas light-intensity physical activity–related metrics were not. These findings highlight intensity-related and short-bout walking patterns that warrant further investigation but do not support specific behavioral recommendations because of the cross-sectional study design.

featuredDrafts.title: Exploring the future of digital health services for older adults in Iran using the GBN scenario planning method
featuredDrafts.abstract: Population aging is one of the most important demographic transitions of the twenty-first century and is creating new demands for health and social welfare systems. In Iran, rapid population aging, expanding digital transformation, and persistent inequities in access to care have made the future of Digital Health Services (DHS) for older adults increasingly uncertain. This study aimed to explore plausible future pathways for the development of DHS for older adults in Iran using the scenario planning approach by Global Business Network (GBN) method.  This exploratory qualitative futures study was conducted in three phases using the GBN scenario planning method. In the first phase, five Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) were held to identify factors influencing the future of DHS for older adults in Iran. These factors were organized according to the STEEP (Social, Technological, Economic, Environmental, and Political) framework into social, technological, environmental, economic, and political dimensions. In the second phase, an expert panel scored the identified factors according to importance and uncertainty. In the third phase, a scenario-building workshop was conducted to develop future scenarios based on the key scenario-driving axes, where the intersecting axes formed the basis of a two-dimensional scenario framework generating four distinct future scenarios for the 2035 horizon.  A total of 70 variables influencing the future of older adult care were initially identified, of which 20 key variables remained after consolidation and expert evaluation. The findings identified Governance and Political–Economic (G-PE) support, together with the Technological Advancement and Innovations (TAI), as the two principal drivers shaping future scenarios of older adult care in Iran. Based on these drivers, four plausible scenarios were developed.  The future of older adult care in Iran will depend not only on TAI but also on the strength of G-PE integration. The scenarios showed that technology can either improve care quality and accessibility or intensify inequality and system fragmentation, depending on institutional capacity and regulatory effectiveness. The study highlights the need for a national integrated roadmap to align governance, digital platforms, and health and social care policies toward resilient, equitable, and human-centered older adult care systems.

featuredDrafts.title: The role of gender in informant reports of cognitive decline in the United States and Mexico
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.  Using data from the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS-HCAP) (N = 3,025) in the United States and the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (Mex-Cog) (N = 1071) in Mexico, we examined informant reports of cognitive decline with 17 questions from the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSI-D). Ordinary least squares regression was used to analyze the gender of respondents and informants in each country for the total CSI-D score and logistic regressions for each individual CSI-D question, controlling for correlates of direct and informant measures of cognition.  There was no significant relationship between respondents’ gender and total CSI-D reports in either country. Female informants in the United States reported 0.57 more CSI-D symptoms compared to male informants while in Mexico they reported 1.35 fewer symptoms. Discussion Our  show that informant gender is associated with systematically different reporting patterns depending on the national and cultural context in which the assessment takes place. The  suggest that informant reports of cognitive decline may represent social norms in addition to actual cognitive decline.

featuredDrafts.title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons
featuredDrafts.abstract: Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.

featuredDrafts.title: Development and Validation of the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) Scale: A Three-Study Investigation of Perceived Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism in Clinical Care
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Ageism in healthcare contributes to undertreatment, dismissive communication, and age-based exclusions from care, yet no psychometrically validated, patient-reported measure captures older adults’ perceptions of age-based bias during clinical encounters. We developed and validated the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) scale. Research Design and  Items adapted from four validated discrimination measures plus two new items were administered to community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older in three independent, predominantly non-Hispanic White samples (Ns = 223, 349, 361) recruited through Prolific within the United States. Study 1 examined latent structure with exploratory factor analysis; Study 2 tested and refined the structure with confirmatory factor analysis; Study 3 confirmed the refined model and evaluated reliability, measurement invariance across gender, and construct validity.  Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 2 indicated that a 20-item model fit poorly and that removing three items produced a refined 17-item model. Study 3 confirmed this model (CFI = .926, RMSEA = .058, SRMR = .057), with excellent reliability for Interpersonal Ageism and the total scale, good reliability for Institutional Ageism, full scalar invariance across gender, and coherent discriminant and convergent validity.  The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.

featuredDrafts.title: Multidimensional Losses and Mental Health of Older Adults in Puerto Rico in the Aftermath of Hurricane Mária
featuredDrafts.abstract: Natural disasters often deprive older adults of essential resources such as food, housing, and finances. Hurricane María devastated Puerto Rico in 2017. This study examines the types of losses experienced by older adults and the association of these losses with mental health 2 years later. We conducted face-to-face interviews with 154 older adults between 2019 and 2020 and found that two-thirds suffered home damage, and 47% lost food. We used latent class analysis to identify three typologies of loss: home damage, displacement, and multi-loss. Older adults who experienced home damage reported better mental health outcomes compared to those in the multi-loss group. Our findings suggest that the types and configurations of post-disaster loss can have different long-term effects on mental health, emphasizing the importance of addressing both essential basic needs and other forms of loss in disaster recovery efforts.

featuredDrafts.title: Age, Resilience, and Hope Predict Daily Functioning After a Flood
featuredDrafts.abstract: We examined associations among resilience characteristics, risk factors, and self-reported functional impairment using archival data from persons exposed to the 2016 flooding in Baton Rouge, LA. Three flood exposure groups were compared: non-flooded (controls), single disaster (flooded in 2016), and double disaster (flooded in 2005 and again in 2016). The Barkley Functional Impairment Scale (BFIS), a self-report measure of daily functioning, was the primary outcome measure. The single disaster group reported more problems in daily functioning than did the non-flooded controls. Correlations revealed that older age was associated with greater resilience and fewer risk characteristics. Regression analyses confirmed that age, resilience, and hope were associated with greater daily functioning after key sociodemographic factors and risk variables were accounted for. Strategies for managing the long-term impacts of multiple disasters for people who live in geographic areas that are prone to severe weather events are discussed.

featuredDrafts.title: Implementing Dementia-Friendly Videos in Everyday Care: A Qualitative Study of Frontline Staff Experiences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Dementia-friendly videos are adapted audiovisual resources designed to support care for people living with moderate to severe dementia. Although evidence suggests these videos can enhance comfort, engagement, and communication, little is known about how frontline healthcare providers integrate them into everyday practice. This qualitative implementation study examined the barriers and facilitators experienced by frontline healthcare providers when implementing dementia-friendly videos in real-world clinical environments. The videos were introduced over an 18-month period in two contrasting care settings in Vancouver, Canada: an acute hospital geriatric unit and a long-term care dementia unit. Nineteen interdisciplinary healthcare providers, including nurses, care aides, and rehabilitation and recreation staff, participated in semi-structured interviews and focus groups after using the videos in routine care. A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted, followed by a later-stage comparison with relevant constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). A participatory research team, including people living with dementia and family caregivers, contributed to study design, interpretation, and theme refinement. Findings showed that time pressures and staffing constraints limited workflow compatibility, particularly because many residents required assistance to operate devices. Limited equipment and unstable internet access further hindered consistent use. Facilitators included motivated staff who acted as catalysts for adoption, the perceived advantages of dementia-friendly videos over general platforms, and staff observations of positive impacts on emotional regulation and participation. Seeing benefits in practice, such as calming distressed patients, reinforced continued use. The study highlights the importance of integrating dementia-friendly videos into existing workflows rather than treating them as additional tasks. Ensuring adequate equipment, supporting motivated staff, and attending to cultural and linguistic relevance are essential for sustainable implementation. These findings offer practical guidance for embedding person-centred digital tools into dementia care.

featuredDrafts.title: Mapping Namaste Care Training for Staff in Long-Term Care Settings: A Scoping Review
featuredDrafts.abstract: Namaste Care is a person-centered intervention for people with dementia in long-term care, particularly those in advanced stages. However, evidence on how staff are trained and supported to deliver Namaste Care remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map training content, delivery formats and support, and training-related outcomes. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, eight databases were searched from inception to May 2026, with additional website and citation searches. Data were synthesized descriptively, and training-related outcomes were mapped against the Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation Model. Eleven studies were included. Training commonly addressed core Namaste Care principles and activities, and several programs also included knowledge of dementia and palliative care, as well as communication and relational care skills. Face-to-face workshops and in-service sessions were the most common delivery formats, with some programs also incorporating experiential learning. Follow-up support and practical resources were frequently reported, and family involvement was incorporated into several programs. Staff reactions were generally positive. Learning-related outcomes included greater understanding of the purpose and delivery of Namaste Care and reported improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and self-perceived skills. Some studies reported changes in staff practice, although intended program frequency or duration was not always achieved because of staffing and organizational constraints. Resident, staff, and family caregiver outcomes were mixed and could not be attributed to training alone. Namaste Care training is therefore better understood as part of a broader practice-support strategy rather than as a stand-alone educational activity. However, existing evaluations remain incomplete, with limited evidence linking staff learning to subsequent practice change and wider outcomes.

featuredDrafts.title: Compound Disaster Exposure and Preparedness Among Older Adults: The Amplifying Role of Caregiving Responsibility
featuredDrafts.abstract: Older adults are especially vulnerable during disasters, yet the factors influencing their preparedness remain underexamined. This study investigates whether exposure to compound disasters (multiple, overlapping hazard events within a year) is associated with greater preparedness among older adults and whether caregiving responsibilities moderate this relationship. Using data from the 2022 and 2023 FEMA National Household Surveys ( N = 4,075), we employed multivariable logistic regression to assess the impact of compound exposure and its interaction with caregiving status on preparedness.  show that compound exposure increased the likelihood of being well-prepared, and caregiving responsibilities intensified this effect. These associations remained robust after controlling for demographic, socioeconomic, and psychosocial factors, including coping appraisal and information-seeking behavior. The findings suggest that caregiving may function as a motivator, enhancing protective action in high-risk contexts. Tailored preparedness initiatives that engage older caregivers may be critical for advancing disaster resilience in aging communities.

featuredDrafts.title: Continuing the Role: Lived Experiences of Family Caregivers after Placement of a Relative With Dementia in Residential Care
featuredDrafts.abstract: Placement of a relative with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) in residential care is often assumed to reduce caregiver burden. However, little is known about how informal caregivers experience their role after placement. This descriptive phenomenological study explored the lived experiences of 9 informal family caregivers whose relatives with ADRD resided in residential care settings. Semi-structured interviews lasting 60 to 120 minutes were conducted and analyzed using Colaizzi’s method to identify the essential structures of post-placement caregiving. Brief quantitative measures, including the CES-D-10 and the Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire, were collected to contextualize participants’ emotional burden. Six themes emerged: emotional dissonance after placement, cognitive load and decision fatigue, persistence of caregiver identity and responsibility, fragmented systems and resource gaps, crisis-driven transitions, and the need for post-placement support. Participants described caregiving after placement not as an endpoint, but as a reconfigured role marked by ongoing emotional labor, vigilance, advocacy, and decision-making. Although physical caregiving tasks had shifted to staff, caregivers remained deeply involved in monitoring care quality, managing communication, responding to crises, and serving as the primary emotional anchor for their relatives. Quantitative findings reinforced these accounts, with all participants scoring above the CES-D-10 clinical threshold and reporting substantial caregiver distress. Taken together, the findings suggest that caregiving continues in sustained and multidimensional ways after residential placement. Residential care settings should recognize family caregivers as ongoing partners and provide structured orientation, clearer communication pathways, and psychosocial support to address the emotional, cognitive, and relational demands of post-placement caregiving.

featuredDrafts.title: Living Arrangements and Life Without and With Depression in Japan: A Longitudinal Analysis
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study examines how life expectancy (LE) without and with depression differs by living arrangement among older adults in Japan, with particular attention to gender differences.  Data were drawn from the Nihon University Japanese Longitudinal Study of Aging (1999–2009). Multistate life table  were used to estimate LE spent without and with depression among adults aged 65 years and older across different living arrangements.  Pronounced gender differences were observed in the relationship between living arrangements and depression-based health expectancy. Men living alone experienced the longest duration and the highest proportion of their remaining lives with depression, whereas among women, these patterns were observed among those living with their spouse. Discussion Living arrangements shape depression-based health expectancy differently for older men and women in Japan, highlighting the need for gender-sensitive policies that address the social contexts in which they are embedded.

featuredDrafts.title: Personal networks and cognitive health across rural-urban contexts
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. Yet few studies have examined the role of personal social networks in shaping these geographic disparities. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.  We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.  There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging. Discussion The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.

featuredDrafts.title: Bridge jobs and retirement identities: Gendered life course approach to workforce exits among Early Boomers
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender. We examine how gender and Social Security eligibility/receipt are associated with retirement identities, and how these identities are associated with the timing of final workforce exit.  We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.  Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account. Discussion This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.

featuredDrafts.title: Forecasting Assisted Living Facility Demand in Singapore: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average Projections
featuredDrafts.abstract: Singapore’s rapidly aging population presents significant challenges for healthcare planning and long-term care provision. This study applies ARIMA time-series modeling to forecast the number of older adults in assisted living facilities between 2025 and 2035. Using historical population data, nursing home residency figures, and simulated indicators of disability and living arrangements, the model projects assisted living demand rising from 19,741 individuals in 2025 to 29,443 in 2035—a 49.2% increase. While forecasts are conservative due to reliance on informal care from family members and foreign domestic helpers, structural shifts such as smaller family sizes and reduced caregiver availability may drive demand higher. The methodology highlights the importance of accounting for disability prevalence and informal care. Findings underscore the need for strategic planning to expand assisted living infrastructure, workforce capacity, and planning frameworks. Singapore’s case contributes to global literature by illustrating aging trajectories relevant to other developed societies.

archiveRecords.title: Purpose in Life Among Older Adults: A Machine Learning Analysis of Potential Predictors
archiveRecords.abstract: A sense of purpose is a central component of mental well-being in older adulthood. Although many predictors of purpose have been identified, most studies have considered a limited set, leaving their relative importance unclear. The present study addressed this gap by examining a large set of psychological, social, and demographic variables in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults from the Health and Retirement Study. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was used to evaluate 47 predictors. Self-esteem emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by positive affect. The leading predictors were organized into six domains: adaptive self-related beliefs, affective well-being, perceived control, optimism, social engagement, and spirituality/religiosity. Demographic variables were less predictive overall. These findings indicate that individual differences in purpose are associated with a broad set of psychological resources involving self-regulation, interpersonal processes, optimism, and positive affect.

archiveRecords.title: Performance of Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-For-Service Populations
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse (CCW) algorithms are widely used to identify chronic conditions in Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) claims. However, their validity in Medicare Advantage (MA) encounters remains uncertain.  We conducted a cross-sectional study using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare data. We analyzed NHATS Rounds 9 and 11, aged≥65 years, with continuous 24-month enrollment in MA or FFS. CCW algorithms were applied to identify six conditions: arthritis, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, and osteoporosis. Self-reported, physician-diagnosed conditions from NHATS interviews served as the reference standard. Survey-weighted sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and balanced accuracy were compared between MA and FFS.  We included 1,708 MA and 2,239 FFS beneficiaries in Round 9 and 1,472 MA and 1,566 FFS beneficiaries in Round 11. Across both rounds, balanced accuracy was similar between MA and FFS for all six conditions. Diabetes and hypertension demonstrated high sensitivity (0.88–0.94), while arthritis and osteoporosis showed lower sensitivity but high specificity. Although statistically significant MA–FFS differences were observed for select metrics (diabetes PPV in Round 9; chronic lung disease specificity in Round 11), absolute differences were minor and not clinically meaningful.  CCW algorithms perform comparably in MA and FFS Medicare data. These findings support the validity of using CCW algorithms in MA encounter data for epidemiologic research for risk adjustment, facilitating more generalizable studies of the growing MA population.

archiveRecords.title: Performance of Claims-based Frailty Indices in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Despite growing enrollment in Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, the performance of claims-based frailty algorithms, which were developed for Medicare fee-for-service (FFS), remains unclear in MA.  We calculated the Kim claims-based frailty index (CFI), Veterans Affairs-Frailty Index (VA-FI), and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) and MA data. We evaluated their performance against the comprehensive geriatric assessment-based frailty index (CGA-FI) and the frailty phenotype (FP) in Round 11 and Round 9.  Among 1,527 FFS and 1,457 MA beneficiaries in Round 11, frailty prevalence was 34.2% and 35.5%, respectively, by CGA-FI ≥0.25, and 13.3% and 16.2%, respectively, by FP. Across FFS and MA populations, the CFI, which prioritizes specificity and positive predictive value, classified 10-12% of the overall population and 30-36% of those with prior hospitalization as frail, whereas the VA-FI and HFRS, which emphasize sensitivity, classified 53-71% of the overall population and 56-87% of those with prior hospitalization as frail. Although claims-based frailty measures performed similarly across FFS and MA populations, their discriminatory ability was higher for CGA-FI ≥0.25 (C-statistics: CFI, 0.79-0.82; VA-FI, 0.77-0.82; HFRS, 0.63-0.77) than for FP (CFI, 0.71-0.77; VA-FI, 0.67-0.75; HFRS, 0.60-0.74). Performance was consistent by race and survey rounds, with modestly better discrimination in women than men.  Claims-based frailty measures are scalable tools for contemporary FFS and MA populations. However applying published thresholds led to differences in frailty prevalence and model performances. Thresholds should therefore be tailored to the intended.

archiveRecords.title: Multimorbidity patterns and domain-specific intrinsic capacity impairments among rural older adults: a multiple correspondence analysis and k-means clustering study
archiveRecords.abstract: Multimorbidity is prevalent among older adults, but its specific patterns and differential associations with impairments across intrinsic capacity (IC) domains remain under-explored. This study aimed to identify stable multimorbidity patterns in rural older adults using multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) combined with k-means clustering and to examine their independent associations with domain-specific IC impairments.  This cross-sectional study included 3,641 community-dwelling older adults with multimorbidity (≥ 2 of 15 chronic conditions) from rural China. MCA was used to reduce dimensionality, followed by k-means clustering to identify multimorbidity patterns. Multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, education, income, and smoking status, was used to estimate the associations between the identified patterns and impairments in each of the six IC domains (cognition, physical function, vitality, psychology, hearing, and vision), with the high metabolic burden pattern used as the reference.  Five stable multimorbidity patterns were identified: high metabolic burden (36.4%), musculoskeletal degenerative (28.4%), gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern (13.8%), cardiovascular-heart failure pattern (13.0%) and respiratory pattern (8.4%). Compared with the high metabolic burden pattern, the gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern was associated with higher odds of vitality impairment (OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.30–2.21); the cardiovascular-heart failure pattern was associated with higher odds of physical function impairment (OR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.11–1.77); and the gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern, cardiovascular-heart failure pattern, and respiratory pattern were all associated with higher odds of psychological impairment (ORs from 1.61 to 2.27). The respiratory and gastrointestinal-tumor risk patterns were also associated with higher odds of hearing and visual impairments. Notably, the high metabolic burden pattern demonstrated the strongest risk for cognitive impairment.  Distinct multimorbidity patterns are differentially associated with specific IC domain impairments. These findings support pattern-oriented risk stratification and targeted functional management in older adults, offering a practical framework for precision geriatric care in resource-limited rural settings.

archiveRecords.title: Prognostic value of mNUTRIC and nutritional indices, including early change, for ICU mortality in older adults with AECOPD
archiveRecords.abstract: Malnutrition is common in older adults with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission and is associated with adverse outcomes. We aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) and its early change (ΔPNI) for predicting ICU mortality and to compare their performance with the modified Nutrition Risk in the Critically Ill (mNUTRIC) score.  This single-center retrospective study included 319 older adults (aged ≥ 65 years) with AECOPD admitted to the ICU. PNI was calculated at admission and on day 3, and ΔPNI was defined as the difference between these values. The mNUTRIC score was calculated at admission. The primary outcome was ICU mortality. Discriminative performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression, and survival was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses.  ICU mortality was 19.8%. The mNUTRIC score demonstrated strong discriminative ability for predicting ICU mortality (AUC 0.852), significantly higher than that of PNI (AUC 0.664; p p p = 0.083), and this was consistent across multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analyses. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly poorer survival among patients with high risk (mNUTRIC ≥ 6) (log-rank p  In older adults with AECOPD requiring ICU admission, baseline multidimensional risk assessment using the mNUTRIC score was strongly associated with ICU mortality. Among patients who survived and remained in the ICU until day 3, early changes in PNI did not provide meaningful additional prognostic information beyond the baseline assessment. The lack of prognostic significance of ΔPNI was consistent across ROC, multivariable logistic regression, and Cox survival analyses. The apparent inverse association between hypertension and mortality was largely explained by disease severity. Further prospective studies incorporating direct measures of frailty are needed to validate these findings.

archiveRecords.title: Dental Coverage and Dental Care Utilization Among Medicare Advantage Beneficiaries With and Without Diabetes United States
archiveRecords.abstract: To examine dental visits, dental coverage, and out-of-pocket (OOP) dental expenditures among Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollees with and without diabetes.  We analyzed 2015–2019 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey data for MA enrollees aged ≥65 years ( N = 12,312). Outcomes included any dental visit, any OOP expenditure, and total OOP spending among those with positive expenditures. Multivariable regression models examined associations between diabetes, dental coverage, and utilization outcomes.  Diabetes was associated with lower odds of having a dental visit (AOR = 0.84), whereas dental coverage was associated with higher odds of dental visits (AOR = 1.85) and zero OOP expenditures (AOR = 3.36). No significant interaction effects were observed between diabetes and dental coverage.  Dental coverage alone may be insufficient to improve dental care utilization among adults with diabetes. Integrating oral health into chronic disease management may improve dental utilization among older adults with diabetes.

archiveRecords.title: Life Course Neighborhood Socioeconomic Disadvantage and Chronic Disease Accumulation in Mid- to Late Adulthood
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examines associations between neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage during adolescence and early adulthood and chronic disease accumulation in mid- to late life.  Using Panel Study of Income Dynamics data linked to U.S. Census and American Community Survey data, we identify four trajectories of neighborhood disadvantage, namely persistent disadvantage, increasing disadvantage, decreasing disadvantage, and persistent advantage, and estimate their associations with chronic and cardiometabolic conditions diagnosed between ages 40 and 75.  Compared with persistent neighborhood advantage, persistent and increasing disadvantage are associated with chronic disease burden, net of individual and contemporaneous neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. Associations between decreasing disadvantage and multimorbidity are largely attenuated after adjustment for individual socioeconomic characteristics.  Persistent neighborhood disadvantage is associated with greater chronic disease accumulation, while worsening disadvantage is particularly associated with cardiometabolic burden, highlighting the relevance of earlier-life inequality for aging. Adolescence and early adulthood may represent sensitive periods, with early adulthood potentially more consequential for chronic disease burden.

archiveRecords.title: DNA methylation variability provides a complementary epigenetic signature of aging heterogeneity: Findings from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging and the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Human aging does not follow a single trajectory. Epigenetic changes offer insight into the heterogeneity in aging by reflecting the combined influence of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors on the timing and progression of age-related changes beyond what chronological age alone can explain. Recent studies in cancer and aging underscore the importance of methylation variability as a marker of biological dysregulation.  We investigated the role of DNA methylation in aging heterogeneity by performing epigenome-wide differential methylation and variance association analyses in blood samples from 1,445 Canadians aged 45 to 85 from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging.  We identified 448 differentially methylated regions and 488 differentially variable regions associated with health decline as measured by the health deficit accumulation Frailty Index, cognitive function, and physical function. These two classes of regions showed minimal overlap, with distinct gene coverage, suggesting that variability contributes a complementary signal to aging heterogeneity. Genes overlapped by differentially methylated regions were enriched for immune and inflammation-related pathways, whereas differentially variable regions highlighted additional localized, CpG‑island–enriched signals shared across health domains, consistent with regionally structured rather than diffuse dysregulation. By integrating significant CpGs from both analyses, we constructed an epigenetic biomarker. The biomarker was associated with all-cause mortality and showed higher discrimination than biomarkers constructed from differential methylation or variability alone, with a similar pattern reproduced in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.  These findings suggest that DNA methylation variability may provide a complementary dimension of epigenetic aging and support further evaluation in larger cohorts with more mortality events.

archiveRecords.title: Hypertension knowledge, medication adherence, and BP control in community-dwelling hypertensive older adults: a cross-sectional study
archiveRecords.abstract: Hypertension affects 31.6% of Chinese adults, yet medication nonadherence (30-50%) remains a critical barrier to control. The purpose of this study is to explore the relationship between hypertension knowledge, medication adherence, and lifestyle factors, and their associations with blood pressure control in older hypertensive patients living in the community.  Cross-sectional study of 437 hypertensive patients (≥ 65 years) in Taizhou, China (Oct-Dec 2023). Medication adherence was assessed via composite score (0–8, > 6 = good) from four validated questions. Hypertension knowledge was evaluated through structured questionnaires. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.  Only 35.3% demonstrated good adherence. Intentional non-adherence behaviors (skipping doses, stopping when asymptomatic) and difficulty remembering medications were significantly associated with poor blood pressure control (p  Poor medication adherence, driven primarily by intentional behaviors (e.g., dose skipping, stopping when asymptomatic) and regimen complexity, is strongly associated with poor blood pressure control. Effective interventions must address these specific behavioral and systemic barriers to improve hypertension management in older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Development and Temporal External Validation of a Parsimonious, Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Predicting 6-Month Mortality in Long-Term Care Facilities: A Retrospective Cohort Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Early mortality after long-term care facility (LTCF) admission is common; yet, prognostic tools are often derived from Western minimum dataset-based cohorts or require hospital electronic health record linkages that are unavailable at intake in many LTCFs. There is also limited evidence on explainable, admission-feasible machine learning–based prognostication in Asian LTCF settings.  The aim of the study is to develop and temporally externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting 6-month all-cause mortality among older adults newly admitted to LTCFs in Taiwan using routinely collected LTCF assessment data.  We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the JUBO Long-Term Care Database, a nationwide private administrative registry covering 636 LTCFs (37.4% of the national LTCFs) in Taiwan. We included residents with first-time LTCF admission and prespecified nonoverlapping cohorts for temporal validation: development (January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2023; n=23,901) and external validation (January 1 to December 31, 2024; n=6216). The outcome measure was death within 180 days of admission. We compared a nonlinear ensemble model (hybrid of extreme gradient boosting and random forest [HybridXGBRF]) with 7 other algorithms, including tree-based and linear benchmarks. Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]), classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, and F 1 ), and calibration (Brier score and calibration plots) were assessed. Model interpretability was examined using Shapley Additive Explanations.  In the development cohort, 5272 of 23,901 (22.1%) residents died within 180 days. In the 2024 temporal validation cohort, 1781 of 6216 (28.7%) residents died. In internal cross-validation, HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models (0.89, 95% CI 0.88‐0.89). In temporal validation, HybridXGBRF maintained strong discrimination (AUROC 0.90, 95% CI 0.89‐0.91), with an accuracy of 0.85 and an F 1 -score of 0.68. Calibration plots indicated close agreement between predicted and observed risks across most probability ranges, with mild divergences at higher predicted risks. Shapley Additive Explanations analysis identified frequent hospitalizations within 6 months, activities of daily living impairment, and weight loss as influential predictors. The model showed stable AUROC across sex and age strata (0.89‐0.90) and maintained high discrimination among residents with improving activities of daily living scores (AUROC 0.91, 95% CI 0.90‐0.92).  An interpretable machine learning model using routinely collected Taiwanese LTCF assessment data achieved strong discrimination, acceptable calibration, and stable temporal validation performance without requiring hospital-based electronic health record linkage. The HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models, but performance differences from extreme gradient boosting were small. The model may serve as a risk-stratification tool to help identify residents who could benefit from structured care review, advance care planning, or palliative care assessment. Prospective implementation studies could determine its impact on care processes and resident- or family-centered outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: Conditional pathways to loneliness in older adults with vision impairment: A decision-tree analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: and  The prevalence of vision impairment continues to increase globally due to population growth and aging. Among older adults with vision impairment, loneliness is common. Prior studies assessing loneliness risk have relied on regression-based approaches, which may not capture complex, heterogeneous conditional pathways. We apply a theoretically guided machine learning approach to examine loneliness risk among older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Research Design and  Using baseline data from 210 adults with AMD (Agemean = 80.1 years) enrolled in a randomized controlled trial, we applied a decision tree method using measures of legal blindness, emotional responses to vision loss, social life satisfaction, anxiety, depression, optimism, future planning, and sociodemographic factors to investigate heterogeneous pathways to loneliness.  Decision tree models demonstrated stable discrimination (AUCtrain=.88, AUCtest=.78, DeLong 95% CI: 0.68–0.88) and robust classification performance across thresholds. Social life satisfaction emerged as the primary branching condition differentiating loneliness outcomes. Distinct pathways suggested that high social life satisfaction was strongly associated with lower loneliness; optimism served as a compensatory resource when social satisfaction was lower. Additional pathways highlighted the effects of vision loss severity, anxiety, and emotional responses to vision loss on loneliness. Depressive symptoms differentiated loneliness outcomes within a lower-anxiety branch, suggesting depression may overshadow protective factors.  These findings suggest that loneliness arises through heterogeneous psychological pathways rather than single risk factors. By identifying conditional configurations of psychosocial and health-related factors, interpretable decision-tree models may inform more targeted screening, evaluation, and intervention strategies.

archiveRecords.title: Neighborhood Deprivation and Nursing Home Staffing Gaps Relative to the 2024 U.S. Federal Minimum Staffing Standards
archiveRecords.abstract: The 2024 U.S. federal minimum staffing rule for nursing homes was vacated and repealed before taking effect, but states continue to adopt their own standards. Whether uniform standards impose uneven compliance burdens is unclear.  To examine whether the 2024 federal minimums differed by neighborhood deprivation.  Cross-sectional analysis of 9,315 U.S. nursing homes linking CMS-reported staffing (April to June 2025) with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI).  Overall, 42.8%, 67.0%, and 31.3% of facilities staffed below the registered nurse (RN), nurse aide, and total nursing minimums, respectively. Facilities in the most deprived tercile staffed 0.103 RN hours per resident day lower than the least deprived (95% CI, −0.161 to −0.045), with 2.28 times the odds of falling below the RN minimum.  Uniform staffing standards would concentrate compliance burden on facilities serving deprived urban communities. Future state or federal standards should pair minimums with financing and workforce supports.

archiveRecords.title: Oral Health Indicators as Important Predictors of Frailty in Korean Adults Aged 50 Years and Older: A Sex-Stratified Explainable Machine Learning Approach
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty is a major public health concern, yet oral health indicators are rarely incorporated into prediction models.  To develop sex-stratified explainable machine-learning models for frailty prediction.  Cross-sectional data from 12,302 adults aged ≥50 years (KNHANES 2016–2019) were analyzed. Frailty was defined using a modified Fried phenotype, with robust and prefrail participants combined as non-frail. Five algorithms were developed separately for men and women and evaluated on independent test sets. Top-performing models were interpreted using SHAP.  The survey-weighted frailty prevalence was 14.1% (95% CI, 13.3–14.9). Test-set AUROCs ranged from 0.73 to 0.78 in men and 0.75 to 0.81 in women. XGBoost was selected for interpretation. Chewing and speaking difficulties ranked above hypertension in both sexes. Chewing difficulty showed complementary support in removal analyses. Smoking status and toothbrushing after meals ranked more prominently in men, whereas unmet dental care need and mouthwash use ranked more prominently in women.

archiveRecords.title: “Someone’s Acknowledged My Mum…in that Moment she Connected”: A Qualitative Study of Family Benefits of Elder Clowning for Persons With Dementia in Long-Term Care
archiveRecords.abstract: Elder clowning is a multi-component, person-centred intervention delivered to persons living with dementia in long-term care to enhance quality of life through individualised social engagement. Although persons with dementia are the target recipients of the intervention, their families may also derive benefits. However, their perspectives currently remain unexplored. This study aimed to explore whether and in what ways families of persons living with dementia in long-term care benefit from elder clowning interventions, from the perspectives of families and long-term care staff. Semi-structured interviews with family members of persons living with dementia and long-term care staff were conducted in four long-term care homes in Eastern Australia. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed according to Braun and Clarke’s Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Analysis of family member ( n = 11) and staff ( n = 20) perspectives on elder clowning generated two main themes: (1) transforming the emotional experience of visiting and (2) strengthening family connections through the shared experience. Elder clowning supported families to have improved visiting experiences with their relative in long-term care, which eased visit-related stress before, during, and after visits. Person-centred engagement through elder clowning was perceived to support the reciprocal interaction and happiness of their relative, which supported positive emotions for families. Families learned about their relative’s communicative capacity and new dementia-specific communication skills, which they then implemented independently from elder clowning. Shared positive experiences supported socialisation, reminiscence, and memory-making, which may have supported family connections. Elder clowning also provided families with opportunities for social support. While some families were actively involved, others preferred to watch, and some were perceived to decline involvement. Families expressed preferences or suggestions regarding intervention delivery, such as continuity and access. The benefits of elder clowning were found to extend beyond entertainment to support psychosocial wellbeing of families of persons living with dementia in long-term care.

archiveRecords.title: Longitudinal Trajectories of Hospitalizations in U.S. Older Adults with Heart Failure
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Little is known about long-term risks of hospitalizations among heart failure (HF) older adults at a national level. We identified long-term patterns of hospitalizations following the diagnosis of HF and assessed whether high-risk patients can be identified prior to discharge.  This is a retrospective cohort study from 2010 to 2020. Fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF during an inpatient stay and followed for up to 5 years. Group-based trajectory models (GBTM) identified 4 trajectories of all-cause hospitalizations during follow-up. LASSO regression was used to identify patients’ baseline characteristics to predict their hospitalization trajectories. Model discrimination was assessed using C-statistics and calibration was evaluated using expected-to-observed ratios.  Of the 84,597 Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF (mean age: 77.4 [± 7.1] years and 58.3% male), we identified 4 distinct trajectories of hospitalizations: Group 1 (n = 19,340; 22.9%) had consistently “low risks” of hospitalization, Group 2 (n = 53,922; 57.9%) had elevated risks shortly after discharge (“high-to-low risk”), Group 3 (n = 5,035; 9.8%) had elevated risks at later stages of illness (“low-to-high risk”), and Group 4 (n = 6,300; 9.4%) had consistently “high risks” of hospitalization. Models were well-calibrated predicting hospitalization trajectories (compared to low-risk patients [Group 1]), and C-statistics were 0.65 (Group 2), 0.68 (Group 3), and 0.79 (Group 4). Discrimination was consistently better among patients ≤70 years and calibration remained excellent across all subgroups with expected-to-observed ratios near 1.0.  High-risk HF patients could be identified at the time-of-diagnosis using routinely available clinical characteristics, enabling targeted interventions during critical periods to improve long-term outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: High obesity rates and mismatch between BMI and waist circumference in older adults: sex-specific patterns from the NutriCare study
archiveRecords.abstract: Purpose Anthropometric thresholds used to define obesity and central obesity are largely derived from younger populations, although aging is accompanied by marked alterations in body composition and fat distribution. We investigated age- and sex-specific patterns of body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC) in very old adults and evaluated how these measures relate to glucose metabolism.  In this cross-sectional analysis of the NutriCare study, 387 relatively independent residents aged 65–101 years from 20 nursing homes were assessed. Standardized anthropometry was performed, and body composition was estimated using bioimpedance spectroscopy. Obesity was defined using WHO BMI criteria, and central obesity using established WC cut-offs for Caucasian populations. Associations with fasting glucose and documented type 2 diabetes (T2D) were examined separately in men and women.  Participants (220 women, 167 men; mean age 81 ± 8 years) had a high burden of excess adiposity, with central obesity more frequent than BMI-defined obesity. Advancing age was accompanied by reductions in BMI in both sexes, with declining fat mass in men and decreasing WC in women. The correlation between BMI and WC attenuated with increasing age. Both adiposity indicators were associated with higher fasting glucose concentrations, while a higher prevalence of documented T2D was observed only among participants with BMI-defined obesity.  In very old adults, central obesity is common, yet the relationship between BMI, WC, and metabolic risk may differ from patterns observed in younger populations. These exploratory findings suggest that the diminishing agreement between BMI and WC at higher age may indicate that conventional anthropometric thresholds do not fully capture adiposity-related risk in late life. Further research in larger and more diverse cohorts is needed to inform age- and sex-specific approaches to obesity assessment in older adults. Trial registration The study was registered in clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05389618) on 25.05.2022.

archiveRecords.title: Quality and safety of large language model–generated medication review outputs in geriatric pharmacotherapy: a two-stage comparative vignette-based benchmark evaluation
archiveRecords.abstract: Polypharmacy and multimorbidity make medication review in older adults a high-stakes clinical task. Large language models (LLMs) may support medication review, but whether item-level concordance with explicit prescribing criteria reflects expert-rated reasoning quality and safety prioritisation is uncertain. We compared the quality and safety of outputs generated by three LLMs using a two-stage evaluation framework.  In this two-stage comparative vignette-based benchmark evaluation, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro responded to 20 standardised geriatric pharmacotherapy vignettes representing fictional older adults aged 72–88 years across four clinical domains. Each vignette contained three potentially inappropriate medications and one clinically relevant START-type omission anchored to the AGS Beers Criteria and STOPP/START version 3. Models received an identical master prompt under default end-user settings; memory features were disabled where available and separate sessions were used for each vignette. Two geriatricians, blinded to model identity, independently rated anonymised outputs using a 100-point rubric comprising medication review output quality (0–80) and critical safety-risk prioritisation (0–20). Stage 1 assessed answer-key concordance; exploratory Stage 2 characterised clinically contextualised error patterns. Comparisons used Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Cochran’s Q, and exact McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction.  Stage 1 concordance was uniformly high, with limited between-model discrimination. Expert-rated total scores differed across models ( p r = 0.55–0.61). Safety scores showed the same ranking ( p r = 0.52–0.62). Reliability of averaged total ratings was high (ICC(A,2) = 0.935; 95% CI 0.897–0.957). In the exploratory Stage 2 error analysis, Gemini was less frequently flagged than GPT-5.2 for superficial reasoning, weak emphasis on life-threatening risk, and any flagged error, and less frequently than Claude Sonnet 4.5 for weak emphasis on life-threatening risk and any flagged error.  Within this vignette-based benchmark, high item-level concordance did not ensure high expert-rated output quality or safety prioritisation. Models also differed in safety prioritisation and in the pattern of flagged errors. These findings support supervised use of LLMs and evaluation approaches that assess reasoning and prioritisation as well as target detection. They should not be interpreted as evidence that one model is clinically superior in real-world practice. Trial registration Clinical trial not applicable.

archiveRecords.title: WHO-ICOPE–Aligned Multidomain Interventions for Intrinsic Capacity in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Systematic Review of Randomised Controlled Trials
archiveRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) reflects older adults’ physical and mental abilities, and its decline predicts loss of independence. The WHO Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) framework promotes multidomain, person-centred interventions, but evidence from trials remains limited.  To synthesise findings from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating WHO-ICOPE–aligned interventions in community-dwelling older adults.  Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (PROSPERO CRD420250654375), five English-language RCTs published from January 2020 to December 2025 were included. Participants had decline in at least one IC domain. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and findings were narratively synthesised due to heterogeneity.  One trial implemented the full ICOPE pathway; four used partial approaches. Improvements were most consistent for locomotion and vitality, while cognitive and psychological findings varied and sensory effects were generally limited. No consistent advantage of full over partial implementation was established.  Evidence remains limited and heterogeneous; further high-quality trials are required.

archiveRecords.title: Aging-Related Diseases in the U.S. Population: A Data-Driven Approach Using All of Us Electronic Health Record Data
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Aging is the strongest risk factor for most chronic diseases, yet aging-related diseases (ARDs) lack consistent, data-driven definitions. Prior work has proposed frameworks to classify ARDs based on age-specific onset patterns, but applications have largely relied on demographically homogeneous populations.  We extended a data-driven framework integrating unsupervised clustering and actuarial modeling to electronic health record data from 633,547 participants in the U.S. All of Us Research Program. Age-specific onset rates for 274 high-burden diseases between ages 21 and 74 were analyzed. Standardized onset curves were grouped using hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Aging-related patterns were assessed with Gompertz and Gompertz-Makeham (GM) models to quantify age-dependent increases in disease onset.  Eleven clusters of disease onset trajectories were identified, with four main clusters encompassing 96.0% of diseases. Two clusters exhibited pronounced late-life increases in onset rate, while one showed earlier but moderate age-related increases, and another displayed largely age-independent patterns. Cardiovascular diseases and cancers were enriched in clusters with strong aging-related onset trajectories. Overall, 165 diseases demonstrated strong evidence of being aging-related, characterized by positive Gompertz age coefficients and good GM model fit. Median onset ages varied across clusters and disease categories and showed statistically significant discrepancies compared with U.K. populations.  In a large, racially diverse U.S. cohort, we identified distinct ARD clusters with shared age-related onset patterns. These findings extend prior work to a more diverse population and support integrated clustering and actuarial approaches to systematically define ARDs and inform aging research and public health strategies.

archiveRecords.title: Application of artificial intelligence to electronic health record data in long-term care facilities: a scoping review
archiveRecords.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to electronic health record (EHR) data in hospital settings, its use in long-term care (LTC) facilities remains unexplored. Limited information technology infrastructure and unique challenges in LTC settings require a comprehensive examination of AI’s potential to enhance care quality and operational efficiency. This scoping review aimed to identify and map current AI applications utilizing EHR data in LTC facilities to inform future research and practice.  The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews was used as a guideline to structure the review topics. The protocol of this scoping review was registered on the Open Science Framework. The inclusion criteria were EHR (participants), AI (concept), and LTC facilities (context), with no date restrictions, but limited to original articles published in English. A systematic search was performed on MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library databases, and SCOPUS by information specialists.  The search included original articles published in English up to October 10, 2024. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Most were retrospective studies ( n = 7), alongside two longitudinal and one development study. AI  included natural language processing, machine learning algorithms (e.g., XGBoost, Random Forest), Bayesian networks, and rule-based reasoning. Applications focused on predicting outcomes such as dementia-related symptoms, malnutrition, pressure injuries, delirium, falls, frailty, urinary tract infections, mortality, and nurse staffing optimization. Data sources included large-scale EHR datasets from nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and senior care communities, often containing over 1,000 resident records or 30,000 clinical notes.  AI applications in LTC settings show promise for enhancing predictive accuracy and care quality. However, current evidence is limited, and further research is needed to improve model generalizability, validate  prospectively, and integrate AI into routine practice in diverse aged care environments.

archiveRecords.title: Exploring the Role of Race and Ethnicity in Resident-to-Resident Aggression: A Qualitative Study
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Resident-to-resident aggression (RRA) is the most common form of elder mistreatment in long-term care settings. Although race/ethnicity is likely a contributing factor, research has been limited in examining the role of residents’ race and ethnicity in RRA. We sought to define and qualitatively examine the predisposing factors and acute precipitants of race/ethnicity-related resident-to-resident aggression (RE-RRA). Research Design and  Guided by the socioecological model, events-based perspective, and conceptual work on stigma-based aggression, we developed qualitative interview and data analytical guides. We conducted nine focus groups and twelve in-depth interviews with 81 nursing home staff from multiple clinical and non-clinical roles across two long-term care facilities on the U.S. East Coast. We coded qualitative data using a deductive thematic qualitative approach.  RE-RRA appeared to be a recurring interpersonal dynamic, though its full scope is likely under-detected and under-recognized. We identified five major types of RE-RRA, including physical violence, microaggression, social exclusion, and avoidance. Ten predisposing factors and eight acute precipitants uniquely contributed to RE-RRA, highlighting the importance of considering distinct race- and ethnicity-related elements in prevention research. We summarized our findings in a conceptual framework for RE-RRA that may be useful for future research.  RE-RRA is a distinct phenomenon shaped by identifiable predisposing and precipitating factors, offering opportunities for future prevention and intervention development. These findings underscore the importance of integrating RE-RRA within staff education, existing clinical governance structures, including incident reporting, and quality improvement processes.

archiveRecords.title: Identifying Palliative Care Consultation Outcomes in Nursing Homes: Insights from Key Partners
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Palliative care (PC) consultation outcomes in nursing homes (NHs) are often assessed using health systems' clinical and utilization metrics rather than outcomes from the perspective of the key partners who provide and sustain it. This study was designed to identify meaningful PC consultation outcomes from the perspectives of NH staff, PC consultants, and NH/PC agency directors. Research Design and  Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the team conducted semi-structured interviews with key partners from 14 NHs in the Eastern United States. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using conventional content analysis.  Participants (N = 33) included NH staff (e.g., primary care providers and nurses), PC consultants (e.g., PC physicians and PC nurse practitioners), and leaders (e.g., NH directors and PC agency directors). Key partners reported meaningful outcomes in four domains: resident, family, NH staff, and NH facility. Resident outcomes included goal-concordant care, symptom management, hospitalization rates, and understanding of care choices and control. Family outcomes included shared decision-making, understanding of the resident’s disease trajectory and management measures, and feeling supported. NH staff outcomes included capacity to provide high-quality care and emotional support. Lastly, NH facility outcomes included filling care gaps, facility reputation, and organizational morale.  These findings highlight multi-domain and interdependent PC consultation outcomes across residents, families, staff, and NH facilities that may be overlooked in existing evaluation frameworks. Future interventions and quality measures should incorporate these outcomes and ensure that residents’ and families’ perspectives are represented.

archiveRecords.title: Living History, Fading Minds: Dementia as the Gateway to Historical Past in South Africa via Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019)
archiveRecords.abstract: This manuscript analyzes the literary, social and cultural representations of dementia in Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019). I contend that the authors’ accounts of their mothers’ struggle with dementia, from its onset to its end, function as living archives of personal and national history. I employ life writing, aging studies, and, to a lesser extent, historiography to examine the literary, social cultural, and historical dimensions of such experiences. I address the narrative construction of the mothers’ identity in later life by highlighting the role of archives and family memories in the context of contemporary South Africa. Thus, I aim to illustrate the instrumental role of life narratives in the creation of safe spaces for intergenerational dialogue and reconciliation with a troubled past on a personal and national level. I also contend that humanities-based inquiry brings to the fore the essential aspects of later life, thereby challenging the pathologizing medical in the representation of dementia, which often disregards the reality of old people as vessels of knowledge. Eventually, I showcase that illness life narratives function as accessible repositories of public knowledge that render visible the realities of aging.

archiveRecords.title: Cognitive reserve and everyday functioning in cognitively unimpaired older adults: evidence from the CAN-PROTECT study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Cognitive reserve (CR) is thought to buffer against the clinical manifestation of dementia, preserving cognitive function despite accumulating pathology. However, less is known about how CR relates to the capacity to independently perform activities of daily living (ADL), particularly among cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults. Here, we investigated this association.  Baseline data from 1,571 CU participants (mean age: 64.7±7.6; 81.3% female) from the CAN-PROTECT study were analyzed. A composite CR score was derived from education, occupational complexity, and engagement in cognitively stimulating activities. Functional ability was measured using the Standard Assessment of Global Everyday Activities (SAGEA) scale, capturing cognitive, applied cognitive, instrumental, and basic ADL, and mobility. Negative binomial models examined associations between CR and global and domain-specific ADL, adjusting for age, sex, cognition, behaviour, and physical/sensory limitations. Additional models tested the independent contribution of CR components to functional outcomes. Mediation analyses assessed the effect of CR on quality of life (QoL) through ADL abilities.  Higher CR was associated with lower global ADL impairment (count ratio=0.58, 95%CI: 0.36-0.94, p = 0.027), driven by 49% less impairment in applied cognitive ADL (95%CI: 0.26-0.97, p = 0.038). Among CR domains, education showed the most consistent association with lower impairment across all ADL domains and was indirectly linked to better QoL through improved function.  CR, particularly education, may play an important role in supporting functional abilities and QoL among CU older adults. Enhancing CR may be a promising avenue to promote functional independence and healthy aging, even in the absence of cognitive impairment.

archiveRecords.title: Where the Wildfires Are: Correlates of Disaster Preparedness Among Oregon Assisted Living Communities
archiveRecords.abstract: Assisted living communities (ALs) serve a growing population of older adults with long-term care needs, especially those with Alzheimer’s and other dementias (ADRD), yet their capacity to prepare for hyper-complex climate-related disasters remains underexamined. Using geographic information systems (GIS), we mapped all licensed ALs with the Oregon Department of Forestry’s wildfire hazard scores, and then assessed organizational correlates of preparedness with a representative sample of Oregon ALs ( n = 321). ALs located in higher wildfire risk areas reported greater confidence in wildfire preparedness and were more likely to have received training and taken actions related to defensible space. However, communities serving residents with ADRD, as well as larger, nonprofit, and chain-affiliated ALs, expressed less confidence in engaging residents and implementing disaster protocols. These findings highlight important geographic and structural disparities in preparedness and underscore the need for tailored planning strategies that consider organizational characteristics and the increasing complexity of climate-related emergencies.

archiveRecords.title: Evaluating Differences in Disaster-Related Staffing for Nursing Homes by Ownership Status
archiveRecords.abstract: For-profit ownership has been linked to lower levels and skill composition of nursing home staffing, yet it is unclear whether disasters exacerbate these differences. We identified 914 nursing homes in Hurricane Ian’s path (September 2022), of which 665 (72.8%) were for-profit. We applied a comparative interrupted time series design to compare staffing hours per resident per day (HPRPD) before and after landfall. Before the storm, for-profit facilities staffed 9% fewer total HPRPD than not-for-profits (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.87–0.95), with similar deficits in the employed (permanent staff) (0.88, 95% CI 0.83–0.93) and licensed (0.90, 95% CI 0.86–0.94) categories. Both for-profit (1.04; 95% CI 1.03–1.05) and not-for-profit facilities (1.03; 95% CI 1.02–1.04) increased total staffing in the post-disaster period, driven by employed personnel; the difference in the magnitude of their responses (1%) was not statistically significant. Baseline staffing differences may affect nursing homes’ capacity to meet disaster-related needs.

archiveRecords.title: The Impact of Hurricane Harvey on Home Health Care Delivery for Medicare Beneficiaries
archiveRecords.abstract: Hurricanes can profoundly affect the delivery of home health (HH) services. We examined the impact of Hurricane Harvey on HH care in Texas, linking 2017-2018 patient-level Medicare HH claims with county-level data on disaster declarations from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. We used segmented interrupted time series to estimate monthly HH use changes among 142,416 beneficiaries in affected versus non-affected counties immediately after landfall (level change) and in its continued aftermath (trend change). HH nursing use dropped 16% immediately following hurricane and continued to decrease by 0-2%, statistically significant throughout post-Harvey period in the affected counties. However, similar impacts were also observed in non-affected counties. HH therapy use showed similar decreases, but with a smaller magnitude. Beneficiaries with the lowest function experienced significant larger immediate decreases in HH therapy use in the affected versus non-affected counties. Findings suggest the need to enhance mandatory disaster preparedness regulations in Medicare-certified HH agencies.
