archiveRecords.title: Composition and size of close social networks among older adults in same-sex and different-sex couples
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examines differences in the composition and size of the close social network among older adults in same-sex and different-sex coresidential unions.  Using pooled, probability-based, cross-sectional data from the 2006–2022 Health and Retirement Study, weighted fractional probit and negative binomial regression models were estimated to examine differences in close network composition (proportions of close children, immediate family members, and friends) and network size (number of close ties).  Compared with older adults in different-sex unions, those in same-sex unions reported a higher proportion of friends and a lower proportion of children and immediate family members in their close network, though overall network size was comparable. Supplemental analyses suggested heterogeneity in these patterns. The same-sex versus different-sex gap in friend composition was larger among males than females and was similarly larger among those who were cohabiting than married. Finally, in terms of network size, males in same-sex couples reported smaller close networks than males in different-sex couples, whereas network size was equivalent between females in same-sex and different-sex couples. Discussion Beyond their partners, older adults in same-sex unions cultivate distinctly friend-centered close networks. This pattern reflects a history of intentionally built chosen ties that queers dominant assumptions about who partnered older adults designate as close. These findings affirm the importance of policies and practices that acknowledge diverse family arrangements, particularly those rooted in chosen kinship, as a fundamental step toward achieving social equity.

archiveRecords.title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal , we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.  In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences;  physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.  Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both  metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes. Discussion These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.

archiveRecords.title: Caregiver Involvement in Dyadic Reminiscence Interventions for Persons With Dementia: A Scoping Review
archiveRecords.abstract: Reminiscence improves cognitive functions in persons with dementia (PWD) and strengthens familial relationships. However, the extent of dyadic reminiscence (caregivers’ involvement in delivering reminiscence), which impacts how interventions are designed for optimal home delivery, remains poorly mapped.  This scoping review mapped literature regarding dyadic home-based reminiscence interventions.  Six databases were searched for empirical studies. Two independent reviewers conducted screening and data extraction, followed by descriptive content analysis.  Thirty studies were included. Caregiver involvement formed a “continuum of engagement” across three broad categories: (i) observers of the PWD, (ii) co-creators of shared materials, and (iii) facilitators of reminiscence-based therapeutic strategies. Key outcomes included quality of life, dyadic relational experience, and PWD neuropsychiatric symptoms.  Caregivers should be recognised as active partners capable of shaping and enhancing intervention outcomes. Future research should prioritise exploring home-based reminiscence interventions that integrate caregiver participation as a core design element.

archiveRecords.title: The effects of physical and sensory activities on motor and cognitive functions in the aging brain: a review
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
authors: Sabrina Simplício de Araújo Romero Ferrari
Bárbara Querem Hapuque da Silva Linhares
archiveRecords.abstract: Brain aging characterized by progressive structural and functional changes, including atrophy of the hippocampus and frontal cortex, reduced neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, and disruptions in network connectivity, collectively impairing memory, attention, and executive functions. However, aging is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous process, with variability in decline and preservation of certain cognitive capacities supported by compensatory mechanisms. Neuroplasticity plays a central role in mitigating age-related losses by enabling functional reorganization and maintaining neural connectivity. This integrative review synthesizes evidence on the effects of physical activity, sensory stimulation, and multisystem interventions on brain aging. Aerobic and multicomponent exercise programs, particularly those lasting 8–24 weeks, have been associated with improvements in hippocampal volume, executive function, and mobility. These benefits appear to be mediated by upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, lactate signaling, and cathepsin B, which support synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and cerebral perfusion. Sensory stimulation enhances neural processing through multisensory integration, strengthening connectivity within attentional and executive networks. Combined interventions that integrate motor, sensory, and cognitive components appear promising and may offer advantages over single‑domain approaches, although direct comparative evidence remains limited. Activities such as dance, proprioceptive training, and musical engagement exemplify sensorimotor integration, promoting cognitive reserve. In addition, emerging technologies, including virtual reality and brain-computer interfaces, further support personalized, neuroplasticity-driven rehabilitation. Together, these findings highlight sensorimotor integration as a central mechanism for preserving cognitive and functional capacity and promoting healthy brain aging.

archiveRecords.title: “Uncontrolled Hypertension Among Medicare Beneficiaries in Rural South Carolina.”
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: More than one-in-five older adults live in the rural U.S. Adults living in rural U.S. experience significantly higher hypertension prevalence and cardiovascular disease-related mortality compared to their urban counterparts. To extend the literature and provide real-world evidence, the primary  of this study was to estimate the prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension and to identify factors associated with it among Medicare beneficiaries receiving care in rural South Carolina.  Data were used from the annual review of Abbeville County Medicare patients diagnosed with hypertension between July 2024 and January 2025. Uncontrolled hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg with or without antihypertensive medications. Generalized linear models with a binomial distribution and logit link were used to examine individual, behavioral, clinical, and area-level contextual factors associated with uncontrolled hypertension.  Responses from 813 Medicare beneficiaries with diagnosed hypertension were analyzed: 55.6% females with a mean age (standard deviation) of 73.2±8.48 years. Overall, the prevalence (95% CI) of uncontrolled hypertension was 76.3% (95% CI: 73.2, 79.1). Compared with a healthy weight, being overweight (aOR=2.0; 95% CI: 1.2, 3.3; p = 0.005) or obese (aOR=2.1; 95% CI: 1.1, 2.8; p = 0.010) was associated with higher odds of uncontrolled hypertension. Contrary to previous findings, “most of the time” PA (aOR=1.57; 95% CI: 1.05-2.34; p = 0.027) was associated with a higher likelihood of uncontrolled hypertension compared to no PA.  Our findings highlight a high burden of uncontrolled hypertension in a rural Medicare population, underscore the need for  measures and further studies into the individual, behavioral, clinical, and contextual factors that may contribute to blood pressure control in rural communities.

archiveRecords.title: Disability trajectories in the last years of life: a Swedish longitudinal multi-cohort study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: The patterns and determinants of late-life functional decline are not fully understood. We examined disability trajectories in relation to proximity to death among decedents aged 70 years and older, and investigated their associations with sex, age at death, education, cognitive impairment, and chronic conditions.  Harmonised data from six Swedish longitudinal ageing studies (1997–2016) within the National E-infrastructure for Aging Research (NEAR) were used. Participants who died at age 70 years or older and had data on activities of daily living (ADL) from at least two assessments were included (N = 2294, 62% women, mean age at death 89.8 years [SD 6.5]). ADL limitations (0–5 scale) were analysed across four time intervals before death (0–2, >2–4, >4–6, and 6–12 years). Group-based trajectory modelling identified disability trajectories, multinomial logistic regression examined demographic associations, and generalized estimating equations assessed associations of cognitive impairment and chronic conditions with trajectory membership.  Three trajectories were identified: constantly low (53%), low-sharply increasing (36%), and high-increasing (11%). Women, those with lower education, and individuals dying at older ages were more likely to follow increasing or persistently high disability trajectories. High-increasing trajectory was associated with higher likelihood of cognitive impairment.  For most, ADL limitations remained low until the final two years of life, though distinct trajectories with steady or sharp increases also emerged. Identifying demographic and health-related factors associated with functional decline may inform targeted interventions and help anticipate care needs.

archiveRecords.title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation
archiveRecords.abstract: Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.  This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.  We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired t tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.  Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen dz =0.28; P dz =0.40; P dz =0.42; P P =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638; P =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601; P =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111; P P P =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.  In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.

archiveRecords.title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.  Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).  While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group. Discussion Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.

archiveRecords.title: Older Adults share an agreement on experiences that elicit love: A study of consensus and individual differences in judgments
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Positive social connections are key ingredients for healthy aging. We studied older adults’ shared agreement on loving experiences and individual differences in their decisions-making to unlock critical information about how this developmental group connects socially.  To explore shared agreement on experiences of love, we surveyed a representative sample (N=400) of adults aged 65 years and older in the United States. They evaluated 61 experiences to determine whether older adults believe they typically evoke feelings of love in most people. We used a Bayesian decision tree model to account for individual differences in respondents’ knowledge and decision-making styles when deriving the consensus on these experiences.  We found a consensus among older adults on experiences of love. In addition, individual differences in knowledge on love and decision-making styles were meaningfully linked to person-level characteristics: female participants and those with higher levels of compassion had higher levels of knowledge on the consensus, White male participants and those with higher levels of loneliness were more likely to guess the shared agreement when they were uncertain, and non-White participants were more likely to guess “True.” Discussion Experiences of love for older adults include both romantic and non-romantic settings. Older adults tended to have different knowledge levels regarding the consensus on these experiences. Future research could examine whether fostering compassion or raising awareness about these loving experiences in daily life might improve well-being for older adults. Increased knowledge regarding these experiences may decrease misunderstandings or loneliness by sharing more loving experiences with others.

archiveRecords.title: Mastery moderates the association between cumulative socioeconomic status risk and accelerated biological aging among middle-aged Black American women
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examines how exposure to cumulative socioeconomic status (SES) risk in midlife shapes subsequent biological aging among Black American women and tests whether a sense of mastery moderates these associations.  Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.  Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery. Discussion Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.

archiveRecords.title: Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural indices
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing. Method Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.  Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups. Discussion These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.

archiveRecords.title: Statin use is associated with improved frailty trajectories in people with HIV
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Statins have pleiotropic properties beyond LDL cholesterol reduction, including anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects that may influence biological aging and frailty. The primary  was to compare frailty trajectories in people with HIV using statins for cardiovascular prevention with those not using statins. Secondary  included differences in walking speed, short physical performance battery, and hand grip strength. This observational longitudinal study included people with HIV from the Modena HIV Metabolic Clinic (Italy) with no prior statin use at baseline and at least three frailty index (FI) assessments. Baseline was the first visit with a FI assessment; follow-up was the last visit. Statin users and non-users were matched for follow-up duration. Time 0 (T0) was defined as statin initiation. Frailty was assessed with a 34-item FI. To minimize collider bias, lipid variables were excluded from the FI due to their direct relationship with statin exposure. Frailty trajectories and secondary outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed models. Beta-estimates were multiplied by 100 to improve readability. Among 3,444 people with HIV (69% men; median age 44.7 years), 23.1% initiated statins for primary prevention and 2.0% for secondary prevention. Statin users had a more unfavorable cardiometabolic profile at T0. In adjusted models, statin use was associated with a reduction in FI over time (statin*time interaction β=–2.562, 95%-CI –3.176,–1.987). No associations were observed with secondary outcomes. Statins may improve frailty trajectories, mitigate aging-related decline and preserve physical function in people with HIV, supporting a broader role for statins in HIV care.

archiveRecords.title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity
archiveRecords.abstract: and  As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time. Research Design and  We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.  The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.  Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.

archiveRecords.title: Care Choices Under the Shadow of Trauma: Childhood Trauma, Care Preparation, and Preferences in Later Life
archiveRecords.abstract: Early-life experiences have a lasting impact on individual development and decision-making processes. Yet, the relationship between childhood trauma and care preferences in old age remains poorly understood.  This study aims to examine future care preferences from a life-course perspective, focusing on the mediating role of care preparation.  Data were used from the Panel Study of Ageing and Society (PAAS), comprising 5,007 participants aged 50 years and over in Hong Kong. Aging adults were first identified whether they have clear care preferences and then specified their preferences for formal and informal care.  Aging adults with greater exposure to childhood trauma are less likely to articulate care preferences. Among those who expressed care preferences, childhood trauma is associated with a higher likelihood of preferring formal care. The underlying pathways reveal that care preparation significantly mediated the associations between childhood trauma and care preferences.

reviewRecords.title: Purpose in Life Among Older Adults: A Machine Learning Analysis of Potential Predictors
reviewRecords.abstract: A sense of purpose is a central component of mental well-being in older adulthood. Although many predictors of purpose have been identified, most studies have considered a limited set, leaving their relative importance unclear. The present study addressed this gap by examining a large set of psychological, social, and demographic variables in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults from the Health and Retirement Study. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was used to evaluate 47 predictors. Self-esteem emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by positive affect. The leading predictors were organized into six domains: adaptive self-related beliefs, affective well-being, perceived control, optimism, social engagement, and spirituality/religiosity. Demographic variables were less predictive overall. These findings indicate that individual differences in purpose are associated with a broad set of psychological resources involving self-regulation, interpersonal processes, optimism, and positive affect.

reviewRecords.title: Prognostic value of mNUTRIC and nutritional indices, including early change, for ICU mortality in older adults with AECOPD
reviewRecords.abstract: Malnutrition is common in older adults with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission and is associated with adverse outcomes. We aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) and its early change (ΔPNI) for predicting ICU mortality and to compare their performance with the modified Nutrition Risk in the Critically Ill (mNUTRIC) score.  This single-center retrospective study included 319 older adults (aged ≥ 65 years) with AECOPD admitted to the ICU. PNI was calculated at admission and on day 3, and ΔPNI was defined as the difference between these values. The mNUTRIC score was calculated at admission. The primary outcome was ICU mortality. Discriminative performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression, and survival was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses.  ICU mortality was 19.8%. The mNUTRIC score demonstrated strong discriminative ability for predicting ICU mortality (AUC 0.852), significantly higher than that of PNI (AUC 0.664; p p p = 0.083), and this was consistent across multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analyses. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly poorer survival among patients with high risk (mNUTRIC ≥ 6) (log-rank p  In older adults with AECOPD requiring ICU admission, baseline multidimensional risk assessment using the mNUTRIC score was strongly associated with ICU mortality. Among patients who survived and remained in the ICU until day 3, early changes in PNI did not provide meaningful additional prognostic information beyond the baseline assessment. The lack of prognostic significance of ΔPNI was consistent across ROC, multivariable logistic regression, and Cox survival analyses. The apparent inverse association between hypertension and mortality was largely explained by disease severity. Further prospective studies incorporating direct measures of frailty are needed to validate these findings.

reviewRecords.abstract: Hypertension affects 31.6% of Chinese adults, yet medication nonadherence (30-50%) remains a critical barrier to control. The purpose of this study is to explore the relationship between hypertension knowledge, medication adherence, and lifestyle factors, and their associations with blood pressure control in older hypertensive patients living in the community.  Cross-sectional study of 437 hypertensive patients (≥ 65 years) in Taizhou, China (Oct-Dec 2023). Medication adherence was assessed via composite score (0–8, > 6 = good) from four validated questions. Hypertension knowledge was evaluated through structured questionnaires. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.  Only 35.3% demonstrated good adherence. Intentional non-adherence behaviors (skipping doses, stopping when asymptomatic) and difficulty remembering medications were significantly associated with poor blood pressure control (p  Poor medication adherence, driven primarily by intentional behaviors (e.g., dose skipping, stopping when asymptomatic) and regimen complexity, is strongly associated with poor blood pressure control. Effective interventions must address these specific behavioral and systemic barriers to improve hypertension management in older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Conditional pathways to loneliness in older adults with vision impairment: A decision-tree analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: and  The prevalence of vision impairment continues to increase globally due to population growth and aging. Among older adults with vision impairment, loneliness is common. Prior studies assessing loneliness risk have relied on regression-based approaches, which may not capture complex, heterogeneous conditional pathways. We apply a theoretically guided machine learning approach to examine loneliness risk among older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Research Design and  Using baseline data from 210 adults with AMD (Agemean = 80.1 years) enrolled in a randomized controlled trial, we applied a decision tree method using measures of legal blindness, emotional responses to vision loss, social life satisfaction, anxiety, depression, optimism, future planning, and sociodemographic factors to investigate heterogeneous pathways to loneliness.  Decision tree models demonstrated stable discrimination (AUCtrain=.88, AUCtest=.78, DeLong 95% CI: 0.68–0.88) and robust classification performance across thresholds. Social life satisfaction emerged as the primary branching condition differentiating loneliness outcomes. Distinct pathways suggested that high social life satisfaction was strongly associated with lower loneliness; optimism served as a compensatory resource when social satisfaction was lower. Additional pathways highlighted the effects of vision loss severity, anxiety, and emotional responses to vision loss on loneliness. Depressive symptoms differentiated loneliness outcomes within a lower-anxiety branch, suggesting depression may overshadow protective factors.  These findings suggest that loneliness arises through heterogeneous psychological pathways rather than single risk factors. By identifying conditional configurations of psychosocial and health-related factors, interpretable decision-tree models may inform more targeted screening, evaluation, and intervention strategies.

reviewRecords.title: Oral Health Indicators as Important Predictors of Frailty in Korean Adults Aged 50 Years and Older: A Sex-Stratified Explainable Machine Learning Approach
reviewRecords.abstract: Frailty is a major public health concern, yet oral health indicators are rarely incorporated into prediction models.  To develop sex-stratified explainable machine-learning models for frailty prediction.  Cross-sectional data from 12,302 adults aged ≥50 years (KNHANES 2016–2019) were analyzed. Frailty was defined using a modified Fried phenotype, with robust and prefrail participants combined as non-frail. Five algorithms were developed separately for men and women and evaluated on independent test sets. Top-performing models were interpreted using SHAP.  The survey-weighted frailty prevalence was 14.1% (95% CI, 13.3–14.9). Test-set AUROCs ranged from 0.73 to 0.78 in men and 0.75 to 0.81 in women. XGBoost was selected for interpretation. Chewing and speaking difficulties ranked above hypertension in both sexes. Chewing difficulty showed complementary support in removal analyses. Smoking status and toothbrushing after meals ranked more prominently in men, whereas unmet dental care need and mouthwash use ranked more prominently in women.

reviewRecords.title: “Someone’s Acknowledged My Mum…in that Moment she Connected”: A Qualitative Study of Family Benefits of Elder Clowning for Persons With Dementia in Long-Term Care
reviewRecords.abstract: Elder clowning is a multi-component, person-centred intervention delivered to persons living with dementia in long-term care to enhance quality of life through individualised social engagement. Although persons with dementia are the target recipients of the intervention, their families may also derive benefits. However, their perspectives currently remain unexplored. This study aimed to explore whether and in what ways families of persons living with dementia in long-term care benefit from elder clowning interventions, from the perspectives of families and long-term care staff. Semi-structured interviews with family members of persons living with dementia and long-term care staff were conducted in four long-term care homes in Eastern Australia. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed according to Braun and Clarke’s Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Analysis of family member ( n = 11) and staff ( n = 20) perspectives on elder clowning generated two main themes: (1) transforming the emotional experience of visiting and (2) strengthening family connections through the shared experience. Elder clowning supported families to have improved visiting experiences with their relative in long-term care, which eased visit-related stress before, during, and after visits. Person-centred engagement through elder clowning was perceived to support the reciprocal interaction and happiness of their relative, which supported positive emotions for families. Families learned about their relative’s communicative capacity and new dementia-specific communication skills, which they then implemented independently from elder clowning. Shared positive experiences supported socialisation, reminiscence, and memory-making, which may have supported family connections. Elder clowning also provided families with opportunities for social support. While some families were actively involved, others preferred to watch, and some were perceived to decline involvement. Families expressed preferences or suggestions regarding intervention delivery, such as continuity and access. The benefits of elder clowning were found to extend beyond entertainment to support psychosocial wellbeing of families of persons living with dementia in long-term care.

reviewRecords.title: High obesity rates and mismatch between BMI and waist circumference in older adults: sex-specific patterns from the NutriCare study
reviewRecords.abstract: Purpose Anthropometric thresholds used to define obesity and central obesity are largely derived from younger populations, although aging is accompanied by marked alterations in body composition and fat distribution. We investigated age- and sex-specific patterns of body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC) in very old adults and evaluated how these measures relate to glucose metabolism.  In this cross-sectional analysis of the NutriCare study, 387 relatively independent residents aged 65–101 years from 20 nursing homes were assessed. Standardized anthropometry was performed, and body composition was estimated using bioimpedance spectroscopy. Obesity was defined using WHO BMI criteria, and central obesity using established WC cut-offs for Caucasian populations. Associations with fasting glucose and documented type 2 diabetes (T2D) were examined separately in men and women.  Participants (220 women, 167 men; mean age 81 ± 8 years) had a high burden of excess adiposity, with central obesity more frequent than BMI-defined obesity. Advancing age was accompanied by reductions in BMI in both sexes, with declining fat mass in men and decreasing WC in women. The correlation between BMI and WC attenuated with increasing age. Both adiposity indicators were associated with higher fasting glucose concentrations, while a higher prevalence of documented T2D was observed only among participants with BMI-defined obesity.  In very old adults, central obesity is common, yet the relationship between BMI, WC, and metabolic risk may differ from patterns observed in younger populations. These exploratory findings suggest that the diminishing agreement between BMI and WC at higher age may indicate that conventional anthropometric thresholds do not fully capture adiposity-related risk in late life. Further research in larger and more diverse cohorts is needed to inform age- and sex-specific approaches to obesity assessment in older adults. Trial registration The study was registered in clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05389618) on 25.05.2022.

reviewRecords.title: Quality and safety of large language model–generated medication review outputs in geriatric pharmacotherapy: a two-stage comparative vignette-based benchmark evaluation
reviewRecords.abstract: Polypharmacy and multimorbidity make medication review in older adults a high-stakes clinical task. Large language models (LLMs) may support medication review, but whether item-level concordance with explicit prescribing criteria reflects expert-rated reasoning quality and safety prioritisation is uncertain. We compared the quality and safety of outputs generated by three LLMs using a two-stage evaluation framework.  In this two-stage comparative vignette-based benchmark evaluation, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro responded to 20 standardised geriatric pharmacotherapy vignettes representing fictional older adults aged 72–88 years across four clinical domains. Each vignette contained three potentially inappropriate medications and one clinically relevant START-type omission anchored to the AGS Beers Criteria and STOPP/START version 3. Models received an identical master prompt under default end-user settings; memory features were disabled where available and separate sessions were used for each vignette. Two geriatricians, blinded to model identity, independently rated anonymised outputs using a 100-point rubric comprising medication review output quality (0–80) and critical safety-risk prioritisation (0–20). Stage 1 assessed answer-key concordance; exploratory Stage 2 characterised clinically contextualised error patterns. Comparisons used Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Cochran’s Q, and exact McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction.  Stage 1 concordance was uniformly high, with limited between-model discrimination. Expert-rated total scores differed across models ( p r = 0.55–0.61). Safety scores showed the same ranking ( p r = 0.52–0.62). Reliability of averaged total ratings was high (ICC(A,2) = 0.935; 95% CI 0.897–0.957). In the exploratory Stage 2 error analysis, Gemini was less frequently flagged than GPT-5.2 for superficial reasoning, weak emphasis on life-threatening risk, and any flagged error, and less frequently than Claude Sonnet 4.5 for weak emphasis on life-threatening risk and any flagged error.  Within this vignette-based benchmark, high item-level concordance did not ensure high expert-rated output quality or safety prioritisation. Models also differed in safety prioritisation and in the pattern of flagged errors. These findings support supervised use of LLMs and evaluation approaches that assess reasoning and prioritisation as well as target detection. They should not be interpreted as evidence that one model is clinically superior in real-world practice. Trial registration Clinical trial not applicable.

reviewRecords.title: Application of artificial intelligence to electronic health record data in long-term care facilities: a scoping review
reviewRecords.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to electronic health record (EHR) data in hospital settings, its use in long-term care (LTC) facilities remains unexplored. Limited information technology infrastructure and unique challenges in LTC settings require a comprehensive examination of AI’s potential to enhance care quality and operational efficiency. This scoping review aimed to identify and map current AI applications utilizing EHR data in LTC facilities to inform future research and practice.  The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews was used as a guideline to structure the review topics. The protocol of this scoping review was registered on the Open Science Framework. The inclusion criteria were EHR (participants), AI (concept), and LTC facilities (context), with no date restrictions, but limited to original articles published in English. A systematic search was performed on MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library databases, and SCOPUS by information specialists.  The search included original articles published in English up to October 10, 2024. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Most were retrospective studies ( n = 7), alongside two longitudinal and one development study. AI  included natural language processing, machine learning algorithms (e.g., XGBoost, Random Forest), Bayesian networks, and rule-based reasoning. Applications focused on predicting outcomes such as dementia-related symptoms, malnutrition, pressure injuries, delirium, falls, frailty, urinary tract infections, mortality, and nurse staffing optimization. Data sources included large-scale EHR datasets from nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and senior care communities, often containing over 1,000 resident records or 30,000 clinical notes.  AI applications in LTC settings show promise for enhancing predictive accuracy and care quality. However, current evidence is limited, and further research is needed to improve model generalizability, validate  prospectively, and integrate AI into routine practice in diverse aged care environments.

reviewRecords.title: Cognitive reserve and everyday functioning in cognitively unimpaired older adults: evidence from the CAN-PROTECT study
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Cognitive reserve (CR) is thought to buffer against the clinical manifestation of dementia, preserving cognitive function despite accumulating pathology. However, less is known about how CR relates to the capacity to independently perform activities of daily living (ADL), particularly among cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults. Here, we investigated this association.  Baseline data from 1,571 CU participants (mean age: 64.7±7.6; 81.3% female) from the CAN-PROTECT study were analyzed. A composite CR score was derived from education, occupational complexity, and engagement in cognitively stimulating activities. Functional ability was measured using the Standard Assessment of Global Everyday Activities (SAGEA) scale, capturing cognitive, applied cognitive, instrumental, and basic ADL, and mobility. Negative binomial models examined associations between CR and global and domain-specific ADL, adjusting for age, sex, cognition, behaviour, and physical/sensory limitations. Additional models tested the independent contribution of CR components to functional outcomes. Mediation analyses assessed the effect of CR on quality of life (QoL) through ADL abilities.  Higher CR was associated with lower global ADL impairment (count ratio=0.58, 95%CI: 0.36-0.94, p = 0.027), driven by 49% less impairment in applied cognitive ADL (95%CI: 0.26-0.97, p = 0.038). Among CR domains, education showed the most consistent association with lower impairment across all ADL domains and was indirectly linked to better QoL through improved function.  CR, particularly education, may play an important role in supporting functional abilities and QoL among CU older adults. Enhancing CR may be a promising avenue to promote functional independence and healthy aging, even in the absence of cognitive impairment.

reviewRecords.title: The Impact of Hurricane Harvey on Home Health Care Delivery for Medicare Beneficiaries
reviewRecords.abstract: Hurricanes can profoundly affect the delivery of home health (HH) services. We examined the impact of Hurricane Harvey on HH care in Texas, linking 2017-2018 patient-level Medicare HH claims with county-level data on disaster declarations from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. We used segmented interrupted time series to estimate monthly HH use changes among 142,416 beneficiaries in affected versus non-affected counties immediately after landfall (level change) and in its continued aftermath (trend change). HH nursing use dropped 16% immediately following hurricane and continued to decrease by 0-2%, statistically significant throughout post-Harvey period in the affected counties. However, similar impacts were also observed in non-affected counties. HH therapy use showed similar decreases, but with a smaller magnitude. Beneficiaries with the lowest function experienced significant larger immediate decreases in HH therapy use in the affected versus non-affected counties. Findings suggest the need to enhance mandatory disaster preparedness regulations in Medicare-certified HH agencies.

reviewRecords.title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal , we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.  In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences;  physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.  Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both  metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes. Discussion These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.

reviewRecords.title: The effects of physical and sensory activities on motor and cognitive functions in the aging brain: a review
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
authors: Sabrina Simplício de Araújo Romero Ferrari
Bárbara Querem Hapuque da Silva Linhares
reviewRecords.abstract: Brain aging characterized by progressive structural and functional changes, including atrophy of the hippocampus and frontal cortex, reduced neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, and disruptions in network connectivity, collectively impairing memory, attention, and executive functions. However, aging is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous process, with variability in decline and preservation of certain cognitive capacities supported by compensatory mechanisms. Neuroplasticity plays a central role in mitigating age-related losses by enabling functional reorganization and maintaining neural connectivity. This integrative review synthesizes evidence on the effects of physical activity, sensory stimulation, and multisystem interventions on brain aging. Aerobic and multicomponent exercise programs, particularly those lasting 8–24 weeks, have been associated with improvements in hippocampal volume, executive function, and mobility. These benefits appear to be mediated by upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, lactate signaling, and cathepsin B, which support synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and cerebral perfusion. Sensory stimulation enhances neural processing through multisensory integration, strengthening connectivity within attentional and executive networks. Combined interventions that integrate motor, sensory, and cognitive components appear promising and may offer advantages over single‑domain approaches, although direct comparative evidence remains limited. Activities such as dance, proprioceptive training, and musical engagement exemplify sensorimotor integration, promoting cognitive reserve. In addition, emerging technologies, including virtual reality and brain-computer interfaces, further support personalized, neuroplasticity-driven rehabilitation. Together, these findings highlight sensorimotor integration as a central mechanism for preserving cognitive and functional capacity and promoting healthy brain aging.

reviewRecords.title: “Uncontrolled Hypertension Among Medicare Beneficiaries in Rural South Carolina.”
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: More than one-in-five older adults live in the rural U.S. Adults living in rural U.S. experience significantly higher hypertension prevalence and cardiovascular disease-related mortality compared to their urban counterparts. To extend the literature and provide real-world evidence, the primary  of this study was to estimate the prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension and to identify factors associated with it among Medicare beneficiaries receiving care in rural South Carolina.  Data were used from the annual review of Abbeville County Medicare patients diagnosed with hypertension between July 2024 and January 2025. Uncontrolled hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg with or without antihypertensive medications. Generalized linear models with a binomial distribution and logit link were used to examine individual, behavioral, clinical, and area-level contextual factors associated with uncontrolled hypertension.  Responses from 813 Medicare beneficiaries with diagnosed hypertension were analyzed: 55.6% females with a mean age (standard deviation) of 73.2±8.48 years. Overall, the prevalence (95% CI) of uncontrolled hypertension was 76.3% (95% CI: 73.2, 79.1). Compared with a healthy weight, being overweight (aOR=2.0; 95% CI: 1.2, 3.3; p = 0.005) or obese (aOR=2.1; 95% CI: 1.1, 2.8; p = 0.010) was associated with higher odds of uncontrolled hypertension. Contrary to previous findings, “most of the time” PA (aOR=1.57; 95% CI: 1.05-2.34; p = 0.027) was associated with a higher likelihood of uncontrolled hypertension compared to no PA.  Our findings highlight a high burden of uncontrolled hypertension in a rural Medicare population, underscore the need for  measures and further studies into the individual, behavioral, clinical, and contextual factors that may contribute to blood pressure control in rural communities.

reviewRecords.title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation
reviewRecords.abstract: Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.  This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.  We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired t tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.  Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen dz =0.28; P dz =0.40; P dz =0.42; P P =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638; P =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601; P =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111; P P P =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.  In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.

reviewRecords.title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.  Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).  While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group. Discussion Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.

reviewRecords.title: Mastery moderates the association between cumulative socioeconomic status risk and accelerated biological aging among middle-aged Black American women
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examines how exposure to cumulative socioeconomic status (SES) risk in midlife shapes subsequent biological aging among Black American women and tests whether a sense of mastery moderates these associations.  Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.  Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery. Discussion Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.

reviewRecords.title: Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural indices
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing. Method Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.  Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups. Discussion These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.

reviewRecords.title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity
reviewRecords.abstract: and  As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time. Research Design and  We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.  The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.  Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.
